Suppose a symmetric matrix $A$ has eigenvectors $\vvec_1$, with associated eigenvalue $\lambda_1=3$, and $\vvec_2$, with associated eigenvalue $\lambda_2 = 10$. Notice that $$ (A\vvec_1)\cdot\vvec_2 \amp = 3\vvec_1\cdot\vvec_2 \\ \vvec_1\cdot(A\vvec_2) \amp = 10\vvec_1\cdot\vvec_2. \\ $$ Since $(A\vvec_1)\cdot\vvec_2 = \vvec_1\cdot(A\vvec_2)$ by [prop-symmetric-dot], we have $$ 3\vvec_1\cdot\vvec_2 = 10 \vvec_1\cdot\vvec_2, $$ which can only happen if $\vvec_1\cdot\vvec_2 = 0$. Therefore, $\vvec_1$ and $\vvec_2$ are orthogonal.

More generally, the same argument shows that two eigenvectors of a symmetric matrix associated to distinct eigenvalues are orthogonal.
